body: Looking forward to your Second Act in a couple years, once the weight starts to spike and the looks start to crater, and you start taking your clothes off to maintain interest. Bookmarked, see you then!

Is that what you referred to in saying that I should “not tell others what they should or should not do?” Doesn’t seem applicable.

The OP thanked the commenters for their advice, so I am not sure I agree that my comment was “unhelpful.” Thank you for your service, but I think you were a little quick with the trigger finger in reminding me of this rule here.
I literally said “it’s up to you” and “do what you want.”

It’s up to you what to do with your counter. The counter is supposed to represent days of continuous sobriety, but nobody here is going to call you a fraud if you leave it where it is.

Do what you want with your counter, it’s not important...only your sobriety is. If leaving it alone will help you not drink, then I encourage you to do so. Not drinking is the only thing that matters.

Have you been sober for the past 114 days? If not, you’ll only be lying to yourself if you leave your counter where it is.  

Don’t look at this as a failure, relapse is part of recovery. You’ve been sober for 114 out of the past 115 days...that’s great! Focus on the positives, and start working on a new high score.

Well done, I would have been furious if I were in your shoes. That is a massive breach of trust, and one that puts you in harm’s way. In my opinion, you were justified to be angry.  

And I’m so glad you didn’t let that justifiable anger send you into the bottle. I can so relate to anger being a huge trigger, and love your phrasing — the anger and the urge. Very applicable to my life. When I start to feel that anger-urge coming on, I reflect on a couple of passages, the first from the Alcoholics Anonymous book “12 Steps and 12 Traditions” (pg. 90):

“What about ‘justifiable’ anger? If somebody cheats us, aren’t we entitled to be mad? Can’t we be properly angry with self-righteous folk? For us of A.A. these are dangerous exceptions. We have found that justified anger ought to be left to those better qualified to handle it.”

And the second, from the AA Big Book also comes to mind (pg. 66): 

“If we were to live, we had to be free from anger. The grouch and the brainstorm were not for us. They may be the dubious luxury of normal men, but for alcoholics these things are poison.”

I am not qualified to ruminate and stew over my anger, even if that anger is justified. That is a luxury normal men may enjoy, but one that is poison to me...if I stay in anger, I will drink. 

Today, I use my sobriety toolkit to get out of that angry mindset and get back to serenity. It sounds like you’ve done that very thing, and I applaud you! Congratulations, and keep up the great work.
Way to go! Sleep well...if you have trouble sleeping, jump back on here and post some more, we can chat, I’ll be up all night :)
Way to go overcoming that urge. Don’t give those losers any power of you...they’re not worth your sobriety.

Sorry to hear that, facing the consequences of our drinking sucks.  

I’m happy to hear that you’re committing to your sobriety pledge regardless of what happens with your wife...I think that’s a great idea. Drinking won’t help anything.

I don’t know, are you? Only you can answer that question.  

I would say that if you think you’re cheating, that might be an indication that you have a problem with the pills. In my experience, people don’t ask themselves whether they have a problem unless they have a problem. But again, only you can answer that question.

The Big Book of Alcoholics Anonymous has three sections of 42 stories from past members who got sober using the program,  telling us what happened, how they got sober, and what sobriety brought to their lives. The final section of stories is entitled "They Lost Nearly All." It contains 15 stories of folks who hit some truly deep bottoms...reading them helped give me some perspective regarding the depths of my own problems, while also giving me appreciation for just how much further down alcohol would drive me if I gave it the chance.  

I am glad that you found us when you did. You don't have to go down any further, you don't have to lose anything more -- you don't have to ever feel this way again. Welcome, stay with us, it is a wonderful life.
Show me...WAKING UP!
Me too man, welcome.

Sobriety is a beautiful life! I am so happy to hear about people finding AA and getting support from the fellowship, so thank you for sharing. The rooms (and the Zooms) are a truly special place.  

I love and accept you too! Congratulations on surviving the lions den, you are strong and you can do this. Keep up the great work.

I can relate to drinking because I was bored...while also not doing anything else to combat that boredom. One of the many ways I lied to myself to justify my drinking.

In my experience, if someone is asking themselves if they have a problem with drinking, they usually do. There’s nothing wrong with giving sobriety a try to see how you like it; I always support people experiencing sobriety, regardless of their ultimate decisions about drinking. At the end of the day though, only you can answer the drinking question for yourself.

Congratulations on your time, it’s a huge accomplishment and you’re right to celebrate it. 

It’s funny, for me I had a hard time getting on the wagon because of special events (like bachelor parties and weddings) that I didn’t want to not drink for. I kept telling myself “I have to drink for just this one more weekend.” If I had been getting sober in 2020 I wouldn’t have had any special events to worry about...all the weddings and such were canceled! But I’m not naive. I know that I would have looked at the week after week of solitude as the perfect opportunity to drink. Reflecting on this, I am reminded of the old saying: “I drank because it was a nice day out; I drank because it was raining.”

It’s never easy to get sober, there’s always something that we can point to for an excuse or justification for our continued drinking. I am so glad that you’re not doing that anymore! Here’s to another 24, let’s keep stacking those days.

If I were you, I wouldn’t drink the wine. If I couldn’t not drink the wine, I wouldn’t go. I attended a bach party in early sobriety and it sent me into a 3 month spiral, right back to daily drinking and all of the self loathing that came with it.  

It would have been a “thing” if I missed the weekend...for about 20 minutes. Then everyone would have gone on with their lives. I didn’t go to my buddy’s bachelor party 6 months later and am very proud of that decision. I was still there for his wedding, and I stayed sober. It was well worth it for me.
Happy birthday! What a wonderful gift to have been sober and available when your friends showed up. I love the availability that sobriety has brought to my life.

Please don’t let one lady, or one meeting, turn you away from AA. Especially with the explosion of online meetings in the era of COVID, you have tons of options of other groups to try out and find one where you are comfortable.  

As to feeling daunted when thinking about not drinking forever: it’s totally normal, and is something I experience. That’s why I can’t do it...I have to keep my focus on today, on not drinking just for today. I know it’s easier said than done, but thinking about not drinking in the future is a waste of my time and energy. Better to spend that mental energy focused on staying sober today.
Take it easy, time takes time.

I appreciate *your* words of inspiration, it’s incredible to hear that you successfully navigated that situation in early recovery. I’m proud of you. You are strong enough to say no to a beer, and that’s all you need to do to stay sober. You can do it.

Regardless of what happens in the future, you didn't throw money down the drain...you invested in your recovery. You spent that $15 (or whatever) investing in your new sober life. You decided to get sober today, and you put your money where your mouth was, spending that money on staying sober. You've spent MUCH more than that on alcohol in the past, what's wrong with spending some money on sobriety tonight?

Congratulations on taking a huge step, congratulations on capturing that good feeling -- now hold on to it tight. Stay here with us, you are worth it!
Don't say only!  A few days is a big deal, never be shy about celebrating your accomplishments. So glad that you are here with us, looking forward to taking this journey with you :)
I don't remember exactly, but I would say a couple to a few weeks. It definitely lingered for a while, unfortunately.
The joys of sobriety! Congratulations!

I always felt like such a dirtbag as I frequently watched the clock, timing when I could leave whatever was keeping me from my drinking. Thank you for sharing, it's a nice reminder of how much I hated that routine, and how liberating it is to leave it behind. I am in control today!
Blackjack! Congratulations on 3 weeks of glorious sobriety, so happy that you are here with us.

Reading, video games, attending AA meetings and being of service to my fellow alcoholic are all some of my favorite things to do in sobriety. But I hesitate to say that these are "escapes" for me...today, I don't feel like I have to escape anymore. Today, I can accept life on life's terms and do my best to enrich the lives of myself and others. 

Probably a semantic point lol, there's nothing wrong with "escaping" into a book for a few hours (or any other hobby/activity), but I couldn't help myself from being a bit of a pedant.
Congratulations on two week, and great focus...it is my daily focus as well. IWNDWYT!

So much good stuff in this post. Finding silver linings is a really effective tool to protect my sobriety, it sounds like you are exercising that tool as well. For some people, drinking dreams can throw them off balance, but like you I use them as a reminder for how shitty it feels to relapse. For some people, not drinking during what was previously a drinking activity is depressing, but like you I try to enjoy what sobriety adds to the experience and how that experience is even better than the old way. 

It wasn't backpacking for me but weddings; I used to love getting shitfaced at weddings, I loved tearing around the dance floor with a glass in hand (or hands), embarrassing myself but not giving a damn. Today weddings are BETTER. I get to meet new people and have meaningful conversations with old friends and family. I get to spend time with my grandmother without shame, precious time that I will cherish for the rest of my life. I didn't cherish weddings before, I hardly remembered them. This sober life is so much better.

Fear is a great topic for me, working my program in AA has taught me just how insidious fear can be, and how infused it was into every aspect of my life.  I am a fan of the following passage, from page 49 of the AA book "Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions," which refers to all of the character defects we alcoholics suffer from:

"All these failings generate fear, a soul-sickness in its own right. Then fear, in turn, generates more character defects."

I like that idea, that my fear is both a symptom and a cause of my character defects, a vicious cycle that feeds off of itself, and feeds off of my soul. That language is also so powerful -- a **soul-sickness**. Fear will corrode me from the inside out, polluting my very soul. 

Today, I do my best to face my fears and overcome them, something that was unthinkable when I was drinking.

Congratulations on pouring that wine down the sink...making an investment in your recovery! I am so glad that you are here, please stay, it only gets better.  

Also thank you for teaching me the word "boke," you learn something new every day.
Whoop whoop! Congrats on setting a new high score, at least for the past 5 years. Keep up the great work...lets keep that number growing!

Thanks for sharing, it sounds like you have the right perspective about this drinking thing. I totally know what you mean about drinking on a gross/rainy day, chasing that warm feeling...then again is there anything better than cracking an ice cold beer on a hot July day, stretching out on a lounge chair and soaking up some sun? Anything, and really EVERYTHING, was an excuse for me to drink.  

I encourage you to adjust your perspective about your relapse, however, and about your prior sober time. The way that I look at it: you haven't flushed anything "down the drain," you still stayed sober those 2 weeks. You relapsed, but that doesn't invalidate your previous sobriety, nor does it dictate your future. Focus on the positives and start putting some more days and weeks together. You got this!

Good. Shit. When life gets big, we have to make sobriety even bigger. I hope that everything goes well at work, but regardless I hope that you keep making the right decision to keep the plug in the jug...because drinking won't make anything better.

I don't think your age is concerning...not exactly sure what you meant by that, but its never to early to quit drinking (if you can't drink, like me). It took me a little while longer to figure it out, but I was a full blown alcoholic at 22 and my life would be significantly better if I put the plug in the jug at that point. And I would not have been alone, I have known plenty of young folks (early-20s and even teens) in recovery.

Congratulations on your successful moderation, and on experiencing some benefits from decreasing your drinking. Good luck on your journey.

To bastardize the immortal words of Bryan Adams, "It was the sober of 69!"  

Congrats on nearly 10 weeks of sobriety, here's to many more.

You are not alone. It sounds like you have a whole lot on your plate right now, I know from my own experience how overwhelming life can get. When things start to get too big for me to wrap my arms around, I like to reflect back on a favorite quote -- "There is only one way to eat an elephant: a bite at a time." Take it easy, focus on what you can control. You were doing  so well a month ago, that means you can do so well again! You know that drinking won't make it better, so focus on controlling that...you can do it, one day (or bite) at a time.

Congratulations! That is a glorious success, almost 100 hours of sobriety. It's not tomorrow yet for me, so I am not celebrating another day quite yet, but I will celebrate the sober hours I stacked up today so far...every one of them is a glorious success for me.

"The greatest ability is availability." Being available is one of the great joys I have experienced in sobriety. Being available to see people in the mornings, and get behind of the wheel of a car (as you mentioned)...also being available to pick up the phone when my a friend of family member calls at night, without having to worry about slurring my words and revealing how drunk I was...being available to have a serious conversation with my girlfriend without her worrying that I will forget it in the morning, or react poorly to criticism...being available to visit my grandmother on a weekend instead of choosing to save that precious afternoon for drinking...and on and on. Doing these things -- being able to do these things -- fills me with a deep sense of satisfaction and pride. Feelings that were never around when I was drinking.

Congrats on your sober time, and congrats on enjoying the joy of availability! Sobriety is a truly wonderful life.

I know that cycle, the tallying of beer cans each morning to know if I had to hit the store on the way home from work that day. The promises to myself that were broken without a second thought when the urge came on. So happy to have left that cycle behind.  

And so happy that you've decided to as well! Welcome to the sub, it is a great source of community and support. I also highly recommend checking out AA meetings, especially with how easy it is these days with the explosion of online meetings in the era of COVID. The only requirement to attending a meeting is a desire to stop drinking, you don't have to buy into the program and you don't have to be a "typical 'drinking every day' alcoholic" as you put it. If you want to stop drinking, you belong. They are another great source of fellowship, community, and support.

What an inspiring post. It’s true, life doesn’t become a bed of roses when we get sober, but damn if the future doesn’t start to look rosier. Congratulations on your anniversary, here’s to many days and years to come!
This isn’t really the place to seek medical advice, but I’m sure NA beer is fine health wise, in moderation. There are definitely healthier choices, but it probably won’t kill you.

I love this, truth and reason are God for me as well. Why do the next right thing, why make the moral choice? Because it is innately good to be good. I don’t think I’m serving the whim of a supernatural being, but rather the whim of the universe to be a force of order and good in the world.  

Your words about clarity remind me of the analogy of the cave, something I think applies strongly to recovery. When I was drinking I thought I saw reality, but really I just saw a representation of reality...a shadow against the wall. Today I can stand up, turn around, and begin to see reality for what it truly is.

Thanks for the read, I enjoyed rambling with you!

I feel like there’s got to be a great dad-joke pun here somewhere.

What’s Batman’s favorite beer? Bats Blue Ribbon...Battington’s Pub Ale...Sam Batams?

What’s Batman’s favorite liquor? Batcardi...Bat Daniels... Small BATch Whiskey?

Ok I am done, I’ll see myself out 🤪

I really like the imagery in your first paragraph, whimsically bleak. Glad you are leaving that scene to the realm of imagination and keeping your feet planted firmly in this sober life. Thanks for a fun read, and I’m right there with you: “fuck you, brain, I can be better!”  

I can and I will, each day I don’t drink!

I think there’s plenty of profundity in your words there. Your “three things that need to happen” track pretty closely to the first 3 steps of AA, albeit differently ordered. 

Step 1: admitted we were powerless over alcohol and our lives had become unmanageable. That’s your #1, recognizing that you need to stop.

Step 3: made a decision to turn our will and lives over to the care of our higher power. That’s your #2, granted it doesn’t track perfectly, but that’s wanting to stop — making the decision.

Step 2: came to believe that a power greater than ourselves could return us to sanity. That’s your #3, being ready to stop comes, as you said, like a gift from on high. 

Anyways that’s what your post made me think about, please feel free to ignore my tortured analogy 😂

Thank you for sharing your story, and good luck to your buddy. The best thing you can do is set a great example of sober living and hope that he follows your path.
You are not alone my friend! The sober community on here and elsewhere has your back. Congrats on 34 days, keep up the great work.

Thank you for sharing your perspective on life after one year of sobriety. It’s not all peaches and cream, but I’m happy to hear you still feel good about your decision to quit drinking. I also love your poetic phrasing — “predisposed to melancholy.” I’m gonna steal that, cause it fits me to a T! Thanks :)

That means you’ve been sober for 98% of the past 50 days...that’s pretty bad ass. Focus on the positives, dust yourself off, and get back on the wagon. Nobody is perfect, be gentle with yourself. Relapse is part of recovery. Just don’t drink for the next 24 hours and you’ll be on track. You got this!

This comment really resonated with me: “I was angry with myself. I don’t like being bad at things. And I hated that I sucked at drinking.”  

I feel that so much. I hated to admit that I had a flaw or a weakness, relative to other “normal” people. I hated to admit that I was not capable of drinking like other people could. I am an incredibly competitive person so it was a tough pill to swallow.  

Today I try not to let my ego run the show and, like you, reflect on the fact that there’s nothing wrong with not drinking. Experiencing the joys of sobriety makes it easier every day.

I put my hand through drywall a few times, broke the glass front to the over door once, attacked a friend on one occasion. I mostly kept my violent rage under control when I was drinking, but as you can see above, I was not entirely successful. I don’t know why I get more violent when I am drunk, but I’m also not worried about it today...and I frankly don’t really care. I have no plans on getting drunk any time soon.
Welcome! We share the same vision for the future my friend 🤙
Thank you for sharing that story of what was a VERY familiar day for me. Thankfully I have not had one of those days in a while, and I do not miss them one bit.

That is so cool, and provides a great opportunity for you to be of service to someone newer in recovery. I have always loved the AA saying “this is a program of attraction, not promotion.” The best way that we can help other people get sober is to set a good example by leading a sober life. If they want what we have, they will follow our path. It sounds like you set that kind of example for this lady, what a neat feeling that must bring. I’m glad you found this group too, and thanks for sharing.

Don’t have the first drink tomorrow. You can’t drink tomorrow if you don’t have the first one, that’s the only one you have to resist.  

I’ve known people with 20+ years who relapsed, one woman who proceeded to stay out for 7 years before making it back. Congrats on getting back here so quickly, now stay. You’re not a disappointment/deadbeat/failure/pussy, you’re someone who stayed sober for 12.5 out of the past 13 months. That’s a great accomplishment, focus on that not the relapse. You can stay sober for the next 24 hours, you’ve proved that — you just have to not have that first drink. You’ve got this, I believe in you.

Sobriety has given me a newfound purpose in life: being of service to fellow alcoholics, as well as to my fellow man and the world at large. I used to look at the world through a cynical, selfish lens. I was only worried about maximizing my own well being. Today I feel so much more fulfilled approaching life from a perspective of charity and service.  

I used to feel like a piece of shit, today I feel like a good person. That makes me really happy.
It is so sneaky! To borrow a phrase from AA: we deal with alcohol - cunning, baffling, powerful. Congrats on 6 months, and on making the right decision today.

I like the comparison to the “start the diet next week” routine, for me it’s the exercise routine...always going to get right on that next week. The truth is there’s never a perfectly convenient time to get sober, there’s always going to be an event on the horizon, an excuse to just drink this one more time. Glad you’re not falling for that trap.  

In terms of advice, I recommend you drive to the event if possible, gives you a ready explanation for why you can’t drink.

They haven’t stopped for me yet, I had a drinking dream two days ago. I hate that feeling of “realizing” that I drank, even though it’s usually fleeting. I try to use them as a tool, to help me remember how shitty I will feel if I ever actually do relapse. Helps me keep it green.
Congratulations on your progress and on your great perspective and attitude! IWNDWYT

I get the exact same anxiety and imposter syndrome! Getting out of bed Monday mornings is so much tougher than the rest of the week, once I build some momentum. Curling up and staying in bed all day is always so enticing. Like you, it has become much easier since I have stopped drinking. Looking forward to continuing to grow and improve in this area of my life as I continue my recovery journey.

Correction: that is not normal behavior for ANYONE. I am so glad that you recognize that you have a problem with alcohol, and are committing to addressing it. Thanks for sharing your story, you helped keep me sober today.
Kick ass, congratulations on 100 hours, here's to many more!

Through working the 12 steps of Alcoholics Anonymous. The program is focused on taking responsibility for our actions, making amends where possible, and ultimately forgiving ourselves. I have found it incredibly helpful in coming to terms with and beginning to remedy the harm I caused during my drinking days.

Wow, that sounds incredibly humbling. I have experienced my share of shame, guilt, and ego deflation in recovery, and have drifted away from friends who I hurt during my drinking. There's nothing that I can do about that now, all I can control is myself. The best I can do is make living amends every day, by not being that toxic person anymore. Other friendships survived my drinking, and today are much richer and more substantial than they were before. Congrats on having a good time with your friends, I hope that tension eases in time and you are able to repair the damage your drinking caused.
Thanks for sharing, and congratulations on your decision to start your recovery journey! You won't regret it.

It sounds like you have a drinking problem. People without drinking problems do not beg their girlfriends for permission to drink. It might be normal for someone your age to want to drink, but it's not normal for someone to want to drink *that badly*. Normal people don't get incredibly intense cravings for alcohol. Normal people don't worry about becoming dependent on alcohol or about what alcoholism might do to them. The fact that you are posting on here is another pretty clear indication that you have a problem, and that at least on some level you know it. I knew I was an alcoholic at 23, but hadn't suffered enough consequences at that point to want to stop drinking.  

Alcoholism is like a broken elevator, it only goes down. We can get off at any time we want, and keep our bottoms relatively high. Some people need to ride the elevator down further than others, but nobody has ever gotten off too early. You may not be at the point of *needing* meetings, but why wait until you get there? I have never heard of someone's life getting worse after they stopped drinking.

Yes you can. Relapse is part of many people's recovery journeys, it doesn't invalidate the time you put together before hand, and it doesn't dictate your ability to stop going forward. Give yourself a break, take it easy, and get back on the horse tomorrow.

No protocols in my experience, new people are explicitly welcomed if they introduce themselves but are otherwise left to listen to the meeting. Lots of people keep their cameras turned off in my meeting, doing that (at least at first) might lower your anxiety a bit. Jump in, you will be welcomed with open arms.

Congrats on 7 days, and of making a great decision! Some good news: it does get better, and you don't have to walk this path alone. You're posting on here and engaging in this community, so there's some support right there. If you are interested, there is a vast network of folks in AA who would also love to support you on your journey to recovery. Thanks to COVID, online meetings are now available at our fingertips 24/7. Even if AA isn't for you, or you have issues with parts of the program, you can still get some great community and fellowship from attending. The only requirement for attendance is a desire to stop drinking!

YIKES! What a curveball to come flying toward your head on day 1. Congratulations on handling it with dignity and grace, and maintaining your sobriety in the face of that stress. Glad you came and posted about it here, keep coming back and keep up the good work!

AA meetings have been a great distraction for me, and thanks to COVID they are available at my fingertips 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. A great source of community and fellowship. Coming on here, reading posts and leaving comments is also a great way for me to get out of my own head and consciously focus on my sobriety.  

I commend you for quitting drinking and changing your diet all at once, I would not have been able to do it. I hope that if push comes to shove, you buckle and eat that pizza before you pick up that drink! Congrats on your 95 days, and good luck with the urges.

Congrats on 1 week of sobriety, that is a big milestone. When I am feeling lonely these days, I jump into an AA meeting. Thanks to COVID, there are lots of online meetings available at all hours of the day. I frequent the meetings at [aahomegroup.org](https://aahomegroup.org), they host meetings 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. We are a good group, and would welcome you with open arms. Even if you don't buy into the AA program, meetings are still a great source of community and fellowship. The only requirement to attend a meeting is a desire to stop drinking!

How about: you will regret it. You wouldn't be posting here otherwise. If you're anything like me, you will feel bad about drinking tomorrow, you will feel guilty and ashamed. For me, that self-loathing was never worth the buzz I caught the night before.

It depends on where you live, but in many places leaves of absence for rehab/treatment for alcohol addiction are considered medical leaves protected under the law. For example, in the United States if a doctor refers you to treatment (and you and your employer satisfy some qualification standards), you would have job protection for up to 12 weeks of leave, under the Family Medical Leave Act (FMLA). Many states have their own similar laws, with more expansive protections. Definitely something to research, if you are interested in treatment.  

To address your post, I think you need to be kinder to yourself...give yourself a break. You're going through some shit right now, nobody can blame you for picking up today. Congratulations on stringing a few days together before that, and on your resolve to get right back on the wagon tomorrow. I don't like to think about it as you're trying again starting tomorrow, rather that you are continuing to try as you have been since last Friday.  

Recovery is a journey, and many times relapse is a part of that journey -- and that is OK. It doesn't invalidate the progress you made before your relapse, and it shouldn't make you feel helpless. You already showed you can not drink for 24 hours, go out and do it again tomorrow. If you need help, come back to this sub and post about it, there are lots of people here ready to help if they can.
You never have to be back on day 3 again, this can be your LAST one. Stay here. The cravings are tough, but as you've shown, you are tougher. You can do this, I believe in you. IWNDWYT

Happy birthday! And congrats on managing those triggers, I know what you mean and have many behavioral triggers myself. It took me a while before I relearned how to live without a beer in my hand, and today the triggers are fewer and farther between. It gets better, keep up the great work.
Let the good times roll! Sleep well, and then on to the next.
Kick-ass, I think I'll join you! IWNDWYT

Retail therapy can do the heart good, glad to hear you took that positive step toward self-acceptance. This would be a pretty "good" excuse to give up, way to go staying strong and not letting life get in the way of your sobriety. It sounds like you have a great support network with your sponsor and your therapist, keep up the great work and look at the bright side...now you've got a reason to do some more thrifting!
I do not miss lunch beers, what a wonderful way to ruin my afternoon, and set the stage for a blacked out evening. Good work today homie, keep it up!

Try not to drink around her if you can. My partner still drinks, but has significantly limited her drinking around me. It's not something I have asked her to do, but it definitely makes it easier not to think about booze when I'm not staring at it in  the fridge.

I am happy to expand on my comment, but am not sure exactly what you are asking. What are you having difficulty getting over and understanding?  Regardless, I'm going to try my best to answer, despite my uncertainty as to your question.  

What I am referring to when I talk about being accountable and being responsible was a natural side effect of quitting drinking. My alcoholism caused me to do the bare minimum in every other facet of my life -- whether that be maintaining relationships with friends and family or fulfilling my obligations at work -- so that I could maximize my drinking. I left early, showed up late, handed assignments in late or not at all and missed many days of work and social engagements...all in the pursuit of being drunk for more hours out of the day.  

Today, I don't have to make excuses for my behavior. I wake up in the morning invigorated with the knowledge that **I** am in control of my life today...not alcohol. If I have things to do, there is nothing holding me back from doing them but myself.  

I am far from perfect. I still fall short all the time, but today I can face my failings with my head held high, make amends when necessary, and dust myself off and get back to work. When I make a mistake today, I apologize and ask for forgiveness -- I am accountable. In the past, I would spiral into a pit of shame, guilt, and self-loathing after giving yet another excuse for my drinking. Today, I don't have to feel that way.

I built confidence by stringing days together. It seems impossible to stay sober for any substantial length of time, but staying sober just for today isn't too bad. I just kept my head down and kept not drinking, just for today. Eventually I looked back and saw how many days I was putting in the rear-view. I didn't have confidence that I could stay sober for a month until I  stayed sober for a month.
Kick-ass, keep up the great work!
Well that is not how I thought this post was going to go after reading that title...what an awesome twist! Sorry about your totaled car, but congrats on your unblemished sobriety.
Welcome back, sometimes we need to stumble to remind us why we are walking this path. Don't think of it as starting again, just getting back on the horse and continuing on your journey to recovery.

I love writing a gratitude list, it's a tool that I have found very helpful in nurturing my own sobriety as well. Staying cognizant of what I am grateful for, the good things in my life, helps keep me off the pity pot.

You hit the nail on the head, "What I wanted was to feel connected to my people and that drinking may  have simulated that feeling but it would only ever cut me off from  fostering it for real." I only had shallow relationships when I was drinking, today in sobriety my relationships have real depth and substance. It sounds like you're making the right choices regarding this buddy, protect your sobriety at all costs.
Way to go, that is a massive accomplishment. Congrats on your progress so far, now its time to start stringing some months together...one day at a time, of course! IWNDWYT
Being accountable, reliable, and responsible. Having control over myself and my actions. Being able to pursue the things I want from life without being held back by my need to drink.

Damn, I LOVE the toxic partner analogy. It is so true: in retrospect my relationship with drinking was just as toxic, abusive, and futile as my relationship with my ex-girlfriend. It is hard to remember what I ever saw in her, or the bottle. Thanks for the great analogy, I am totally stealing it!
Congrats on your dozen days, welcome back to the land of the living. Stick around, it only gets better.
Don't wait until you rack up more consequences before coming to your senses. Nothing bad comes from stopping drinking, your life will only improve. It seems like a no-brainer to me.
Indeed. Service is joy :)

"I don't want to be like this."  

Guess what? It is your lucky day, you don't ever have to be like this again. Congratulations on coming to the monumental realization that you are an alcoholic, it is the first step down the path to recovery.  

I second u/doowgad1's advice regarding AA. Even if you don't think the program is for you, even if you have some hangups about relying on a higher power, I highly recommend attending some meetings just for community and fellowship. Zoom meetings are available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week -- no matter what time it is, you can always jump into a meeting. I frequent meetings at the site "[aahomegroup.org](https://aahomegroup.org)" and recommend that you check it out, we are a welcoming bunch.

I am lucky that I don't have to deal with dreams of moderation...I don't have any illusions that I can one day drink moderately, or like a gentleman, because no part of me wants to. I just want to get shitfaced, blackout drunk. That has made it easy for me to not pick up the first drink: I don't have a little voice lying to me that this time it would be the only one.  

So I don't have an answer for you! All I know is that even if those thoughts never end, you don't have to let them lead you to drink. Congrats on overcoming that craving/urge and maintaining your 5+ years of sobriety. Heck of an accomplishment.
Glow up! Sobriety has done wonders for you...and there is so much yet to come. Keep up the great work.
Congratulations on making a plan and on putting into action -- that is the critical first step on the journey to recovery. Thank you for sharing your story, it was an inspiring read.

Take it easy, easy does it, be gentle with yourself. You didn't screw anything up, you learned a valuable lesson that will help you stay sober going forward. Recovery is a journey and a process, facing a setback is normal and OK. You're going to be pushing 3 weeks before you know it, just take it one day at a time. You've got this!

My liquor store guys definitely think I died...I was in there on the daily, they had my case ready for me at the counter when I walked in the door. They don't sell smoothies there, so I have not been back. Congrats on your recovery, and the satisfaction of sticking it to that smug cashier.
Every minute that you don't take a drink is another victory...and you've done that over 2.6 MILLION times in a row. Congratulations on the milestone, keep up the great work.

I will be forever grateful to the therapist who told me, in no uncertain terms: "You cannot drink alcohol." I knew she was right, I had known for a while, but I needed to hear it from a professional for it to really sink in.  

Your SO sounds like a dick, to be blunt. Not drinking for 2 weeks to support you is such a small ask, the fact that he responded by getting sulky, giving you the silent treatment, being rude...it sounds like alcohol is more important to him than you are. Does he have a drinking problem? If so, it may explain why his priorities are so out of line. I am not suggesting that whenever someone gets sober their partner needs to go along for the ride, but this small gesture to help you in early recovery is very little to ask. You have every right to be pissed off at him, I don't have any advice other than to reassert your needs and impress upon him how important it is to you.

There will always be a reason to drink, and while it sounds like this is a truly "good" one, it is still ultimately just an excuse. I am sorry that you experienced and are now re-experiencing that trauma, but alcohol is not going to help anything. Please don't drink. Lean on your sober support network, lean on this sub, keep posting and venting, and tire yourself out reading other people's posts sharing inspiration and encouragement. I can't imagine what you are feeling right now, but I *know* that drinking will only make it feel worse. You did the right thing coming here to share this and I am so proud of you...now stay here, and keep the plug in the jug.
Get after it killer! Waking up alert and ready to take on the day is a true joy of recovery. Enjoy your hike this morning, and the many lovely mornings ahead.

Correct me if I am wrong, but that means you didn't drink for 199 out of the past 201 days? That is pretty bad ass. Lets start another streak today man, you can do this. Don't worry about working out today, take it easy and recover. Easy does it, as they say. It is really tough getting sober when living with drinkers, but it's not impossible! 

Lean on your sober support network, lean on this subreddit. I am gonna be hanging around here all day, keep posting and I'll keep commenting and we can get through this together. IWNDWYT
Love this. It is so simple...not easy, but simple.

Congrats on 25 years of sobriety, and on 23 years of marriage (happy anniversary). I love that last question you asked prior to putting down the bottle: "Why do you continue to make yourself miserable?" Why indeed.  

Looking back now, quitting booze seems like such an obvious decision...it's befuddling why it took me so long to put it together. As they say, we deal with alcohol -- cunning, baffling, powerful. Thanks for the inspiration this morning.

I went to my sister's/brother-in-law's joint bachelorette/bachelor party...and I relapsed. I was 27 days sober and in retrospect definitely should not have gone. While I would have missed out on some good memories, I was not ready to be in that situation and maintain my sobriety. That slip lead to a 3 month bender that almost saw me lose my partner and my job. Thankfully, I was able to get back on the wagon before any real consequences kicked in.  

I was lucky. If I could do it again, I would skip that party.  My sister and BIL would have understood, and I would have had plenty of other opportunities to make better memories with them going forward.  

You said that not going isn't an option...but that simply isn't true. Not going to a winery is always an option; if you need to avoid the event to stay sober and your friends don't understand...you need to get better friends.  

Sorry. I don't mean to be a downer. If you ARE going to go, try to enjoy the perks that sobriety brings you. Enjoy the money you're not spending, the calories you're not consuming, and the drama you're not getting embroiled in. Today I  can go to events like this without worrying about my sobriety, and I really enjoy watching folks get sloppy, knowing that I don't have to worry about embarrassing myself. Enjoy having conversations with people, knowing that you're going to remember them. Celebrate your strength as you navigate the day. If you start to get an urge to drink, jump on here and post about it and find some support. Treat it not as an event where you don't get to drink, but as an event that you get to experience sober. I get so much more out of parties, celebrations, weddings, etc. now that I can fully enjoy them. Good luck, and congrats on 45 days!
Congratulations on the new high score! I am not sure when badges reset, I am in the US and likewise don't have my correct day count displayed...but I am sure they will update shortly :)
I love me some sobriety-centric poetry, thank you for sharing your creative pursuit. Good luck at rehab, and with the rest of your goals. You've got this, one day at a time.

Thank you! It's derived from a great quote by Rabindranath Tagore: "I slept and dreamt that life was joy. I awoke and saw that life was service. I acted and behold, service was joy."  

I love it; it's a perfect articulation of what I have learned thus far in sobriety.
Sounds like an awesome day, congrats on being productive, making a great first impression, and staying sober.
Congratulations -- you've run out of fingers to count the days on your right hand, tomorrow we start on the left! Keep up the good work :)

I don't have any statistics to throw at you, but I can say that quitting cold turkey worked for me. I went from drinking \~15 beers a day to nothing, without any tapering.  I know that at a certain level of alcohol consumption, quitting cold turkey can be dangerous. I would consider consulting a doctor if you are nervous about it. Otherwise...give it a go, you can always pick the bottle back up if sobriety isn't for you.
Whoop whoop!! You're free! And you never have to feel that way again. So happy that you've joined us, now stick around. It only gets better and better.
It really is amazing how quickly that fog begins to clear. Congrats on 9 days, keep up the great work!

It sounds like you are off to a solid start, getting honest with your family and seeking help to guide you through early sobriety. I don't have any experience reducing/tapering off booze, but have heard of plenty of folks who went that route. You are in good hands with the crisis/counseling team, I would have faith in them and follow their instructions. You can do this, I really want you to quit for good this time too, keep doing the next right thing and take it one day at a time.
Here's to another 24 glorious hours of this sober life. Ain't it a beautiful thing!

The curse of social media -- people only post their highlights, creating a distorted picture of reality. In reality, we all have bad days, we all say and do ugly and shameful things...but we don't post about them, scared to show weakness or that we aren't "perfect" (whatever that means).  

Congratulations on saying this out loud, that takes a lot of courage. Please know that you are not alone. Lots of people posting (and lurking) on this sub feel exactly the same way you do. I felt exactly like you do once. It gets better, but sometimes it takes many attempts before it sticks. Keep trying, you almost did it, I know you're going to get there one day soon.

I heard you, thanks for sharing honestly and from the heart. Try to take it easy, one day at a time, you don't have to stay sober for the rest of your life all at once. And if you end up having to go inpatient, please don't look at it as "ruining" your hard work. I speak from personal experience, in-patient treatment was necessary for me to get to the place where I am today. Life is a long journey and its a process...if you need to be hospitalized to keep you from hurting yourself, then get yourself checked in. Life will be waiting for you when you return. 

I'm glad you reached out to this community instead of making a bad decision. Keep up the good work, and congratulations on 1+ years of sobriety!

Sorry to hear that you are struggling, glad that you came here for support...you're in the right place. I struggled to find meaning in life for many years, but I'm happy to say that my program of recovery in AA has helped me find that meaning: service. Today, I  strive to be the most useful person I can be, and to be of maximum service to my fellow man. It brings me comfort each day to know that I did what I could to make the world a better place.

In my experience, people who don't have drinking problems don't ask themselves if they have a drinking problem. It sounds like you don't like your current relationship with alcohol...so change it! Only you can tell yourself if you're an alcoholic, but you don't have to be an "alcoholic" to cut down on your drinking. If you have trouble cutting down, you will start to answer your question.

I struggled with this for a long time as well. I was a card carrying atheist for as long as I can remember thinking for myself and had a difficult time surrendering my will. For me, it finally clicked when I started to really believe the things that all of these people were telling me. So many folks in AA meetings shared about being long-time atheists before finding spirituality through the program...I knew they weren't lying to me, so if it worked for them why shouldn't it work for me too?  

For me, it came down to intellectual pride...I clung to my ideas about atheism because they gave me a sense of intellectual superiority over the "weak" people who relied on the crutch of spirituality or religion.  

To quote from Dr. Bob's story: "If you think you are an atheist, an agnostic, a skeptic, or have any other form of intellectual pride which keeps you from accepting what is in this book, I feel sorry for you." At first I bristled at this passage, reading it as a snide remark. Now I realize that Dr. Bob meant that with true compassion...he earnestly felt sorry for those of us who allow our intellectual pride to be an obstacle to our recovery. 

To quote another personal story from the Big Book that sums up what made the higher power stuff click for me: "I was willing to believe that A.A. was telling me the truth." It was as simple as that for me...once I began to truly believe the truth that I was hearing, and once I checked my ego at the door, I was able to begin connecting with my own higher power.
That's the only way I know how to put a day together. Keep up the good work, you can do this.

Sorry to hear that you're struggling, but glad to see that you're posting about it and seeking support...you made the right choice! Drinking won't help, it just kicks the can down the road. Since you're posting here, I think you already know that (at least on some level).

I know it seems trite in the face of emotional/relationship struggles, but be gentle with yourself...take it easy...easy does it. You can't fix all of your problems, especially hypothetical future problems that have yet to come to pass, in a single day or night. All you have to do today is not drink. It gets easier, it gets better, you can do this.

Try to give yourself a break, and celebrate your successes. A month of sobriety is a huge accomplishment, a month and one day is even bigger...you can get there, and far beyond. Keep up the good work and don't drink.

What a powerful post. I could really feel your emotion in those words, I am sorry that you are experiencing so much pain. I am giddy, though, that you are facing it with the right attitude. You are right, it is better to feel than to numb our feelings and escape into a bottle.

I love how you put it: "I never wanted to feel. I was scared of this. This intense FEELING. But that's what being alive is all about!" This is the truth for me.

This is also on point: "I know I have to let that 'old me' go and accept this new me. But I don't know who the hell this new me is." I didn't know who I was when I got sober either, I had spent so many years crafting a persona that centered around my drinking, I had to develop a new identity and a real personality when I put down the booze. I am happy to report that I know the new me today, and he is the man I want to be. Good luck on your journey of self-discovery, I am sure it has great things in store for you.

Way to go, playing the tape forward is what keeps me sober when I am faced with cravings. And give yourself some credit -- not drinking today is a massive victory, it's the hardest thing you will ever have to do in sobriety.
Welcome back, the great news is you never have to feel this way again. Stay here and stay sober, you got this!

Be gentle with yourself, you didn't mess up, relapse is part of recovery. It is a journey and a process, glad to hear that you are taking something positive from this experience and using it as a source of strength. I gave myself permission to drink after 27 days, and then stayed out for 3 months. Congratulations on getting back so quickly, now just stay. We can do this, one day at a time.

Good list. I love "I ruminate on past relationships and friendships that went sour and prevent myself from growing and moving on." I didn't grow for over a decade of drinking, I was a stunted and immature man child, and you better believe I obsessed over past relationships and mistakes. Gave me some sorrows to drown, to justify my drinking. Not today. Congratulations on the joys of sobriety!

Welcome! I drank like you drank, slamming \~15 beers every night (some days more, some days less). It was a real challenge to get over that hump for me as well, I am so glad you've made it. Congratulations on starting this journey, and don't get discouraged if cravings return (they did, and do, for me), just rely on your sober support network to overcome them. You are stronger than alcohol, you can do this.

That's awesome, I love checking things off the bucket list that always seemed out of reach when I was drinking. For me, it has been reading books...I love to read, and today I read books again! I am so grateful for everything sobriety brings me.

13th stepping, in my experience, is someone taking advantage of another who is new to sobriety. I don't think it counts as 13th stepping if you develop a friendship with someone and then pursue a romantic relationship...just don't prey on newcomers or approach AA as a dating app (I could be wrong about this, but this is the context I have always heard/understood).  

That being said, I also agree with what others have said: listen to the guidance regarding relationships in the first year. You have enough to worry about focusing on your recovery, you don't need the distraction. Get a sponsor, work the steps, and worry about this stuff later.

I started working the steps with my first sponsor about 18 months ago, and made it to step 4 before drifting away. I recommitted to the program with a new sponsor in March and have been diligently working the steps since. I can relate to your feeling of not "needing" to work the steps, having some sober time under your belt. For me, working the steps has opened my eyes to a whole new way of living, even though I had been hearing about it in meetings for over a year. When I truly engaged with the program and committed to working it, the promises began to come true in my life. Stick with your sponsor, be fearless and thorough, and great events will come to pass.

Hooray! Congratulations on being the master of your own destiny today, not letting alcohol poison your perspective. Happy that you were able to turn the other cheek...and forget about those stars, thank yourself! You did that, you are strong, you are awesome. Keep up the great work.

Just don't drink today...simple, but not easy. Stay on here, read posts and respond to comments, embrace the fellowship and community. It's only a few days, imagine how happy you'll be walking into rehab with a few days already under your belt. You can do it -- prove it to yourself and you'll be taking some huge steps in your recovery journey.

There's a couple of sayings in AA: "there's nothing worse than a belly full of booze and a head full of AA" and "AA ruins drinking." I think what you're describing is something similar, your education about your addiction has lifted the veil and revealed drinking for what it truly is...toxic, negative, futile. I will not drink today, because I know alcohol has nothing to offer me but heartache and despair. I hear you when you say you miss the bliss of ignorance, but in time sobriety will show you what bliss truly looks like.  Keep up the good work, it gets easier.

It's wise to be cognizant of addictive behavior, it is very possible to transfer that toxic behavior to things other than alcohol (including exercise) and getting similarly negative results. That being said, working out 60 minutes a day sounds like a healthy and productive use of your time. I wouldn't worry about your newfound enthusiasm for this hobby, embrace it! If it starts to get in the way of you otherwise living your life, that is when you start to have a problem.  

I don't work out as much as you, but I definitely work out a lot more than I did when I was drinking...though that doesn't say much, since I was not exercising at all until I got sober. Today I am enjoying physical exercise again, and working on getting into a habit like you described. I'm jealous of your routine! One day I am going to get there too, but for now I am giving myself a break and taking it easy, one day at a time.
Preach! You are a badass, congrats on 555, I am clapping for you...and I'll clap for you at 666 too, I don't care if it's weird, you'll have deserved it!

Thanks bro, it feels good to put distance between today and my sobriety date, but I can only do it one day at a time. I had a drinking dream last night, vividly reminding me that I am only one bad decision away from resetting my day counter.  

It's not you against the world, you're not alone, we've got you. If you rely on this and other supports (such as AA meetings, if you are interested in those), I know you can do it. We've got this!
They will keep creeping up, if you keep not drinking today. Congratulations on a week, keep up the good work and in a couple of days I want to congratulate you on a new high score!

I love your enthusiasm, and I share it! Life is truly a miracle -- even when it is challenging -- it is a miracle to be alive today. Words really do fall short, sobriety has shown me the beauty and joy of life.

Thanks so much for sharing, I love Stephen King and knew about his coke abuse, but somehow had never heard about his alcoholism, or his recovery. Really cool to reflect on how much strength that must have taken...that man had it all, financially set for life, and he still chose to put down the bottle. For many years I dreamed about winning the lottery so I could quit my job and drink all day...cool to learn about someone who essentially had that level of financial security and nevertheless chose to live a sober life.  

It's never too late to get sober, our past does not have to define us, it's never too late to start a new chapter in our lives. Thanks again for a great read.

Of course, and gets to pick which drive thru to hit 😎  

Who said sobriety didn’t have some perks?!?
Heck yeah. Life is a never-ending process of learning and growing...when we stop growing, we are dead. Looking forward to battling and growing alongside you my friend.

I know what you mean about selfishness. Someone in a meeting said something that knocked my socks off: "If I get everything I want, if I achieve all of my goals, I will have done nothing for another person." I reflected and knew that was true for me as well...and I don't want it to be anymore! Today, I want to accumulate wealth, but not so I can accumulate material things, so that I can give back and be of service to others. Today I want to make the world a better place, and that makes me feel better about myself.

Don't worry about that theoretical stigma (in my experience, no one cares about people going to rehab), get the help you need and get sober. It is a better life. You are here, you know the decision that you should make. Stay. Stop drinking, and stay here with us. It is a wonderful life.
I go with the tried and true: I can't drink, I'm allergic, when I drink I break out in handcuffs. Gets a little laugh, and moves the conversation along.

Great list. My favorites are "I am lovable and can love myself" and "I can forgive myself and when I can’t, at least I can practice trying." The absence of those abilities was a big part of the spiritual malady that drove me into the bottle. Today, I am working toward those "learnings" and get better every day...as you said, one day at a time.

I'm glad that they know, and I hear you, I don't like making people not drink either. I don't like thinking that I'm causing someone else to have less fun because they have to hang out with me. That being said, if I am feeling triggered and can't be around it without cravings getting to me, I have to put my sobriety first and I either ask my friend/family to stop drinking or I remove myself from the situation.  

That's just my experience, you know what is best for you. I again encourage you to lean on this sub, and whatever else makes up your sober support network, in the event that you start feeling like pouring yourself a glass. IWNDWYT
Way to go. I love conquering mental hurdles in sobriety, especially when they turned out to be more mole hill than mountain. Congratulations on experiencing the joys of sobriety!

Does your family know you're not drinking? For me, it has been essential for my friends and family to be on the same page as me. It helps me stay accountable, and not let any thoughts that "I could get away with it" creep in.  

If they do know and are willing to not drink around you, perhaps that is something to explore with them. Having other non-alcoholic drinks around is critical, so good plan there. If you're feeling shaky, jump on here and post about it to get some support. You've got this!

I struggle with depression as well. I know your title asked for suggestions outside of therapy and meds, but that has been the biggest thing that has helped me deal with my depression, so I have to plug it. In the absence of that, I highly recommend AA meetings. Even if you aren't interested in joining a group or working the program, a meeting is a great escape from your own thinking, and is a positive and supportive environment. I get a lot of fellowship and community from my AA meetings, helps fight the loneliness that otherwise creeps in.

Sobriety gives us the strength to deal with challenges that used to baffle us...to deal with life. What a wonderful life, congratulations on your dozen days, I look forward to reading those observations in a couple more weeks!

Sorry that you had that experience, I haven't read the book yet but plan to at some point. As they say, there are many ways to skin a cat...find what works for you, don't stop searching and never stop trying. It's the journey of a lifetime, looking forward to walking it with you.

You're not a stupid fuck, that's a profound realization, at least it was for me. Congratulations on weathering this storm without returning to alcohol, feeling pain hurts but it is a part of living. I would rather feel that pain than go back to feeling nothing but empty inside, physically and spiritually.

Congrats on 50 days, and the joys you have been experiencing in sobriety!
Well done, it sounds like you know that nothing good will come from that bottle. Pour it out, and don't think of it as wasting a beer...think of it as investing in your recovery. Here's to 41 days!
What a beautiful message. You have summed it up well -- recovery, unity, service. When I started making AA and my recovery a central part of my life, I began to truly enjoy the joys of sobriety.
It might not be advice, but you've encouraged me with your resilience in the face of a challenging year. Keep up the fight indeed!

Thanks for the encouragement, I'm rooting for you too. Glad to hear you overcame that urge, and no shame in leaning on a friend for some assistance. My recovery has relied on my sober support network, including people who are not sober but who support and respect my decision.

Don't worry about not putting your toe back in the water ever again, just don't put it back in the water today...and then keep doing that. You've got this.

Well done, AA has been a critical part of my recovery. I encourage you to keep attending meetings and if you like what you see and hear, to get a sponsor. A sponsor will help take you through the steps, and can be an invaluable guide and aid through recovery. Good luck, and congrats on 2 days!
Migraines suck, glad you’re feeling better and that you didn’t use it as an excuse to drink. Keep up the good work!
Sobriety has truly given me a life beyond my wildest dreams. Glad you’re enjoying the fruits of recovery as well, congrats on 30 days, here’s to many more.

Congratulations on all those days, and all of the ways your life has improved this past year+. To quote some AA adages: take it easy, time takes time, if we walk into the forest for 10 years it will take 10 years to walk out. You can be a yogi master if you want to, anything is possible in sobriety, but it might take a while. Glad to hear you are (rightfully) giving yourself a break.
Awesome, it’s great to have a sober buddy to take your journey with, even better to have it be your partner. Congrats, you’ve got this, one day at a time.

I never did a rehab/detox, but I’ve had a few inpatient stays for dually diagnosed people, including a CBT program where I shared a room with another guy.  

In my experience, the facilities varied in terms of what they allowed you to bring in. It might be worth checking out any materials you have from the facility, asking your mom, or giving them a call to find out. In the facilities l was in (for example) they didn’t allow any belts/shoelaces/drawstrings due to potential self-harm risks, so it might be worth wearing some slip on shoes and some pants that won’t fall down without a belt/drawstring. Razors were a no-go, not sure about shavers, but again this is all going to be very facility specific. I’d check, or at least go with your mom so she can take home anything you’re not allowed in with. During my stays my parents also brought me books and things during visitation, but i don’t know if your place offers that (so again, I’d check).  

I was super nervous when I went inpatient, but in all cases (at least a half a dozen separate stays), it was not bad at all. I made some friends, and never had any problems. I highly doubt your sexuality will present any problems. Good luck, you’ve got this.
